title: Your own voice
hookLine: the Prophet ﷺ liked to hear the Qur'an from others (Bukhari)
last: EVERY LETTER IS DUE ITS RIGHT.

lines: I LIKE TO HEAR IT FROM SOMEONE ELSE.
cards: A voice played back on a voicemail or in a video can sound thin and strange, not like its owner at all.
And after yesterday's rules, it would be easy to think the Qur'an belongs to the professionals, the well-known reciters with voices like cellos. A story in Bukhari turns that upside down.
The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, the one the Qur'an was revealed to, turned to a companion and asked him to recite. The companion was baffled. Recite to you?
It was sent down to you. And the Prophet said: I like to hear it from someone else.

teach.h: IBN MAS'UD RECITES, THE PROPHET WEEPS.
teach.b: The companion was Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. He began reciting Surah an-Nisa' and reached the verse that asks how it will be when a witness is brought from every people, and the Prophet himself is brought as witness over them.
The Prophet said: enough. Ibn Mas'ud looked up and saw tears running from his eyes. The one who received the words was moved by hearing them in another man's voice.
Other reports make the same point from different sides.
The Prophet heard Abu Musa al-Ash'ari reciting one night and told him he'd been given a flute, a mizmar, like those of the family of the prophet Dawud, David.
And in Abu Dawud's collection the Prophet says: beautify the Qur'an with your voices.
Not your voice made lovely by the Qur'an: the Qur'an made lovely by your voice.

Scholars draw the line in different places on what that allows, but a common thread runs through them: a beautiful, moving voice is praised, as long as the tajwid is kept and the recitation doesn't turn into a performance of songs.
Another hadith says he is not of us who doesn't recite the Qur'an with taghanni, a word some read as chanting it melodiously and others as being content with it. Either way, the invitation is plain.
The beauty isn't only in the well-known voices. It's also in the ordinary voice that's trying.

how: Muslims recite the Qur'an aloud in prayer, in study circles, and at home; many listen to well-known reciters, and teachers encourage students to recite in their own voice with care and feeling rather than imitating a performance.

o: beautify: make the Qur'an lovely aloud
hurry: get through the Qur'an quickly
be silent: listen while others recite

games.q: who's who in the stories — tap the pairs.
p: given a flute like David's family

s: the Prophet only ever recited the Qur'an, never listened to others
he asked Ibn Mas'ud to recite, saying he liked to hear it from others.
a hadith says to beautify the Qur'an with your voices
scholars all agree on what taghanni means
some read it as melodious chanting, others as being content with the Qur'an.

games.q: you're Ibn Mas'ud. the Prophet asks you to recite to him. what do you say first?
o: of course, and begin at once
recite to you, when it was sent down to you?
games.why: he asked exactly that. the Prophet said: I like to hear it from someone else. then he wept at 4:41 (Bukhari).

practice: Somewhere only you can hear, choose something short: the bismillah, the first line of the Fatiha, or one verse in English if that's what you have.

Say it out loud once, slowly, at a normal volume, not a whisper, and let your voice be exactly what it is. Then sit in the quiet and notice how it felt to hear it in your own voice; if you'd like, say it once more, a little slower.

wordCard.voice: Zayyinu, beautify: what the Prophet told people to do to the Qur'an with their own voices, after he himself asked to hear it recited by others.

orig.note: Arabic: beautify, make lovely. zayyinu l-Qur'an bi-aswatikum.

carryVoice: Your line: beautify it with your voice. Even the Prophet liked to listen. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5050 (Ibn Mas'ud recites an-Nisa'; the Prophet weeps)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5048 (Abu Musa's mizmar of the family of Dawud)
